### Phase I — The advisory war and escalation (Jan 1964 – Jul 1965)

*End of phase against the historical state: POP.night_control +2 to +6 against history (low) · POP.night_control.I_corps 0 to +3 against history (low) · POP.night_control.II_corps 0 to +3 against history (low) · POP.night_control.III_corps +3 to +8 against history (low) · POP.night_control.IV_corps +3 to +9 against history (low) · GVN.political_stability 3–5 (history 4; low) · VCI.strength -20% to -10% against history (medium) · TRAIL.tonnage_arriving -5% to +5% against history (low) · FIND.vci +0.3 to +1 against history (medium) · ARVN.effectiveness.small_unit +1 to +5 against history (low) · ARVN.effectiveness.fire_coordination -4 to -3 against history (low) · ARVN.self_sufficiency.fire_support 0 to +2 against history (low) · US.casualties 1,250–1,335 (history 1,369; low).*

The war that COMUSMACV inherits on 1 January 1964 is an advisory war that is being lost. The coup of 1 November 1963 had killed Ngo Dinh Diem and his brother Nhu, and with them went the province chiefs, the Strategic Hamlet Program and most of the Republic's administrative continuity. MACV under General Paul D. Harkins is a headquarters of advisers, helicopter companies and support troops; about 23,300 Americans are in the country by the end of 1964, none in combat units, and 147 die by hostile action that year [H40]. The fighting is done by the ARVN, the Regional and Popular Forces and the CIDG camps against a Viet Cong movement rebuilt since 1959 on the Viet Minh's old infrastructure and on cadres returning down the Trail.

The phase is a double collapse and a double response. In Saigon the state comes apart, coup after coup, and the generals spend more of their energy on each other than on the countryside. In the field the Viet Cong form regiments and then a division around Saigon, and at Binh Gia, Ba Gia and Dong Xoai they beat the general reserve on ground they chose. Hanoi commits regular PAVN regiments to the South for the first time. Washington answers from the air, first with reprisals and then, from 2 March 1965, with an opening strike on the North's whole target list and a campaign run from Saigon without zones or pauses (EV013-1); and on the ground, from two Marine battalions guarding an airfield in March to the decision of July to fight the war with American troops. Every constraint that will shape the war is drawn here except the one this war never drew, the restricted zones around Hanoi and Haiphong (P013b), and so is the enemy's basic answer to American firepower: close in, choose the time of battle, keep the base areas beyond the border.

Most of what is new in this war stood on its first day, and none of it decided the coups or the summer offensive. The Republic itself was changed by one session of decrees on 1 January 1964: land to the tiller and a Commission Against Corruption with an American power to suspend aid behind it, a resident rural police with a Special Branch, province and district chiefs chosen from a ranked list, Phung Hoang centres built on the police's files, an officer board and a combined command (EVR05-1). Behind those decrees stood what had been built since 1957 and was already in the ranks: every private and territorial trained on the 2026 course, every NCO schooled for his grade, every officer educated before each promotion, and an industry a generation above the country's own (EVR05-1) [M007] [M009]. By July 1965 about 330,000 hectares are titled, the musters have found the RVNAF about 41,000 men smaller than its rolls (EVR05-2) [X-001], and about 1,100 village posts stand in the held belt, where a post with its trained and rearmed Popular Forces platoon now holds about nineteen attacks in twenty (EV002-2) [X-009]. The Front's answer is to move its committees out of the held villages, and the first campaigns of the task force, of Delta and of the district centres follow them out (EVR05-3).

The command can also see and strike as history's could not. The Global Hawk orbit closes the trawler route within a year and moves Hanoi's southern supply to Sihanoukville about eighteen months early (EV003-1); on the night of 4 August 1964 the radar shows no torpedo boats, and Pierce Arrow is not flown (EV000-3). Sixty-four AC-130J gunships fly over the posts from the first week, and by the summer of 1965 the Front has stopped assaulting the posts within their net on clear nights (EV015-1). The B-52Js wait on Guam for sixteen months with a target list and no authority, and then destroy in a week what history's fighter-bombers spent years on (EV013-1). The North disperses, Moscow and Beijing rebuild its sky (EVCP02-2), and nothing that reaches the South changes: the porters, the trucks and the Front's regiments notice nothing at all (F013-7).

**How the phase ends:** By the end of July 1965 the advisory war is over. The 173rd Airborne Brigade and the III Marine Amphibious Force are in the country, the 1st Cavalry Division is preparing to sail, and Rolling Thunder is in its fifth month. The Viet Cong have regiments and divisions around Saigon and on the coast, PAVN regiments are in the Highlands, and the summer offensive has broken ARVN battalions at Ba Gia and Dong Xoai faster than they could be rebuilt, though no battalion of the general reserve has been wiped out. Thieu and Ky have just taken power after a year and a half of coups. In Hanoi the Politburo has committed itself to winning before the Americans arrive in strength, and in October its regiments will go after Plei Me.

Inside the held belt the summer is not history's. About 330,000 hectares are titled to about 270,000 families, rent is no longer paid in most districts the government holds, and there the government's arrival no longer means the landlord's [X-001]. About 1,100 village posts stand, two-thirds of the chiefs have come from the list, about 140 district centres are open behind the posts, and the Front's committees have begun to leave the villages around them, gaining the safety of the contested edge at the cost of the villages' daily obedience (F006-4) [X-006]. Outside the belt nothing has changed except the promise.

The army that enters Phase II is the one 1957 built and 1964 began to reform. Its privates and territorials are trained, its NCOs schooled for their grades and its companies led by the educated classes, at the price of 3,300–5,500 of its best sergeants kept as instructors in the years it could least spare them [X-010]. The board has filled about 70 of some 190 battalion commands and relieved its first nine commanders; the rest, and every general, are the generals' choices, and a third of the battalions are still under captains (F007-8) [X-007]. The general reserve came back from Binh Gia and Dong Xoai with more of its men than on any course before this one, and the Front enters Phase II with 10,000–30,000 of the Republic's carbines and the academy's leader's manual (F010-20) [X-004]. The Directorate's plants run at about half capacity under a domestic share four months old, the coast's Route 1 is open after the worst flood in memory, and the Front has an industrial working class in Bien Hoa to organise [X-008].

The command can see the enemy's rear and not his regiments under the canopy or his cadres in the hamlets. The sea route is closed and Sihanoukville open. The gunships have pushed the Front's attacks into the rain, onto posts beyond their net and into the mortar and the mine, and they changed the nights at Nam Dong and Dong Xoai and not the days (EV015-1) [X-015]. The task force, Delta and the district centres have each broken a committee from one file and seen each rebuilt from the region (EVR05-3). The combined command is a channel rather than a command, its orders passing through the prime minister's office and its allies' through Seoul's countersignature and Canberra's casualty estimate (EV012-3). The North has lost its fixed economy and replaced it with drums, diesels, pontoons and a fighter force living in China, and holds three divisions at home against a landing that is not coming (F013-13) [X-013]. The flow south is untouched, and the American decision of July is history's.

### Phase II — The main force war (Aug 1965 – Dec 1967)

*End of phase against the historical state: POP.night_control 71–76 (history 67.2; medium) · POP.night_control.I_corps 0 to +3 against history (low) · POP.night_control.II_corps 0 to +3 against history (low) · POP.night_control.III_corps +8 to +14 against history (medium) · POP.night_control.IV_corps +6 to +14 against history (medium) · VCI.strength -45% to -30% against history (medium) · ENEMY.engagement_control 61–66 (history 66; low) · TRAIL.tonnage_arriving -12% to -1% against history (low) · FIND.main_force 0 to +3 against history (low) · FIND.vci +1.55 to +3.15 against history (medium) · ARVN.effectiveness.small_unit +2 to +7 against history (low) · ARVN.effectiveness.fire_coordination -6 to -4 against history (low) · ARVN.self_sufficiency.fire_support -5 to +2 against history (low) · US.casualties 8,450–9,070 (history 9,378; low) · US.political_tolerance.public 42–44 (history 44; low).*

Phase II is the American war at full stride. US strength rises from about 184,000 at the end of 1965 to 486,000 at the end of 1967, and American deaths by hostile action from 1,369 in 1965 to 5,008 in 1966 and 9,378 in 1967 [H40]. The big operations win their battles and do not change the war: the Ia Drang, Masher/White Wing, Hastings, Attleboro, Cedar Falls and Junction City each kill men the reports exaggerate and are followed by the enemy's return, because he decides when to fight and withdraws into Cambodia, Laos and the DMZ when the cost is too high. In Saigon the junta survives the Buddhist uprising and wins an election with a third of the vote; pacification is reorganised under CORDS in May 1967; and in Hanoi the militants around Le Duan plan a general offensive for Tet.

Beneath the main-force war runs the one the provisions changed most, the war for the held belt. The land programme leaves the phase with about 820,000 hectares titled to about 640,000 families (EV001-6) [X-001]. With a Special Branch that owns the files, a constable in about 1,500 villages, chiefs who stay, district centres everywhere and Delta's raids, the government's own belt is cleared of resident infrastructure before 1968 rather than after it, and the committees go to govern from the base areas and from across the border by courier (EVR05-4). The Front answers by killing the best chiefs and moving its legal cadres into the towns (EV002-3), and where the method is pushed into villages the government does not hold at night it becomes the historical Phoenix, three years early (EV006-4). None of this alters the main-force war, fought on the borders and in the Highlands where few tenant farmers live. It alters what that war is fought over.

The enemy's rear is now counted rather than guessed. The panhandle watch, the gunships and Delta's road teams count the Trail's trucks from December 1965, and the B-52J cuts every bridge it can measure from April 1966; the enemy answers with fords and pontoons no bomb can close, and by the autumn more is moving than before (EVR05-5, EV005-2). Sihanoukville is measured by March 1967 as the source of most of the arms for III and IV Corps (EV003-4). The northern campaign is the theater's own: the restrike watch keeps the Red River crossings closed more days than not while the cell's monthly kills fall from about 140 to 35, there is no Christmas pause and no POL strike, and this command reports in October 1966 that the North's war in the South needs none of what is being destroyed (EV013-3, EVCP02-4) [X-013].

The armies are better in the fights the enemy grants and get no more of them. Every infantryman carries a modern carbine and every squad a belt-fed gun; the Ia Drang and the Hill Fights cost fewer American lives, and no Marine on 881 South dies beside a jammed rifle (EV000-23, EVCP02-3). The ARVN's battalions are filled from the board's list, its sergeants schooled and its privates trained, and the enemy does what he does against every better unit: he declines to fight it and lays his ambush for the one beside it (EV007-3). He moves his war in the lowlands south of Da Nang to the mine, which no course teaches against (EV009-2), and the devaluation of 1966 sends trained privates home to families their pay no longer feeds (EV007-4). The radio puts every post on the district net, and the Front answers by ambushing the company that answers the call, until the districts learn to answer with guns and gunships rather than trucks (EV008-4).

**How the phase ends:** At the end of 1967 the United States has about 486,000 men in Vietnam and has lost 9,378 killed in the year [H40]. Rolling Thunder has dropped about 864,000 tons on the North [H9], the Trail carries more than ever, and MACV and the CIA dispute whether the enemy numbers 300,000 or 430,000, a dispute over whether the guerrillas and the infrastructure, the part of the enemy the main-force war does not touch, are counted at all [H39]. Westmoreland tells the National Press Club on 21 November that "the end begins to come into view" [H39]. McNamara is leaving. Saigon has an elected government under Thieu, and in Hanoi the Politburo has set Tet for the General Offensive and General Uprising. Each side is certain the other is weaker than it is.

In the held belt the resident infrastructure has been driven out of most villages with settled posts, and its committees govern from the Ho Bo woods, the Rung Sat and Memot by courier, with collections at a sixth to an eighth of 1964's; its legal cadres are in the towns, where the police knows less (EVR05-4) [X-002]. About 820,000 hectares are titled, rent has ended wherever the government holds the night, and the Commission has convicted a general (EVR05-6) [X-001]. Phung Hoang has an audited count of about 18,000 neutralized since 1965, a fifth of them committee members, and the word Phoenix has been a press story since March (EV006-4) [X-006]. The infrastructure is intact in every hamlet the government does not hold after dark, which is still most of the contested countryside.

The enemy's supply is measured, the Trail by the panhandle watch, Sihanoukville by the count and the North's roads by the Gulf watch, and every measure says that what arrives exceeds what his forces in the South need (EVR05-5, EV003-4) [X-003]. The bombers have learned that a bridge they can measure dies in a night and is replaced by five crossings they cannot, and that a siege they can measure becomes the enemy's worst battle (EV005-2, EVCP02-3). Over the North the theater has had the campaign it asked for and the result it predicted, about 40–90 fewer American aircraft lost than historically, and no hearings on restrictions that were never drawn (F013-18) [X-013].

The armies enter 1968 better in the fights they are given. The American army has had no rifle crisis and has lost somewhat fewer men in the first minutes of its fights and in the nights after them; its battalions rotate as units with staggered reliefs that cost 15,000–25,000 spaces in theater, and about 7,000 selected advisers hold every field post below corps (F006-12) [X-006]. The ARVN has about four in five battalions under officers the board chose, its NCOs schooled and its privates trained, and the drill sergeants returning 650–1,800 platoon sergeants a year (F009-4) [X-009]. **About two-fifths to a half of history's ARVN battalions broken in 1966–67 were not broken in this war. The judgment is low-confidence, and the true figure is more likely near two-fifths than a half**, because the officer reforms, the basic course and the NCO schooling each claimed a share from overlapping cases and none checked its cases against the others' (REVR01-1, POSCP04-1) [X-CP04]. None of it shows in a return. The enemy declined the fights that would have shown it, attacked less what kept its routine, and moved his war to the mine in the lowlands and to the unit that still rode (EV007-3, EV009-2). The corps and the generals are what they were, and the palace has a file on the board's officers while COSVN has had every list the board published (EV007-4).

The factories produce what the domestic share buys, short of power and, after Phu Cat, short of their gunners' trust. Every post in the held belt has a radio, and where the guns reach, the first call is for fire, and the post holds itself better than the hamlet around it (EV008-4) [X-008]. The gunships have taken the clear night over the posts of the held belt; the coast's monsoon nights are still the Front's, and the first Vietnamese gunship squadron is flying (EV015-4). The combined command has one corps under a Vietnamese commander and three under American deputies, moving at the speed of the generals the palace chooses (EV012-6) [X-012]. The population of the South, the object of the war, is still largely outside the reach of either army's strategy.

### Phase III — Tet and its aftermath (Jan 1968 – Dec 1968)

1968 is the year the war turns, and it turns on a battle the enemy lost. In the first hours of 31 January PAVN and VC forces attack Saigon, Hue and most of the provincial capitals at once. By the measures of the battlefield the General Offensive fails: there is no uprising, the cities are retaken, and the Viet Cong lose most of the cadres and local forces of a decade. By the measures of politics it succeeds beyond Hanoi's hopes: within two months the President has refused Westmoreland's 206,000 men and withdrawn from the race. US deaths by hostile action reach 14,592, the highest of the war, with about 537,000 Americans in the country at the year's end [H40]. Three offensives, in January–March, May–June and August–September, meet three American answers: Khe Sanh held and the cities cleared, with Abrams in command from June; the decision of 31 March capping the commitment; and the move into the countryside, with mobilization in June, Phoenix and the Accelerated Pacification Campaign. The cost in the South is the heaviest yet: about 630,000 new refugees, more than 70,000 homes destroyed, and 14,300 civilian dead in the first phase alone by the government's count [H39].

In this war the year runs on the same dates and turns the same way, decided in Saigon, Hue, Khe Sanh and Washington. What changes is the Delta, the hamlets and the army that met the offensive. The Front attacks the held belt from a smaller base: its guides do not arrive, the hamlets warn the garrisons, and the district centres take a third of the leaders it sends to direct the uprising (EV000-42) [X-006]. The files held pieces of the warning, and the combined estimate read them as local; the leave order stood (EV012-8) [X-CP03]. The ARVN and the territorials meet the offensive armed, trained, schooled and under the board's commanders, and about a third of the attacks on district towns never get inside the walls; in the cities all of it lowers the cost without shortening the battles, except at Hue, fought under one commander and ended five days early (EV000-44) [X-012]. When the government moves into the countryside after the offensives, about 900,000 hectares are already titled, and Phoenix is only the name Washington learned for district centres that had run since 1964 without quotas and under an audit (EV000-54) [X-001].

Above all this the radar watches the border. At Khe Sanh it measures the siege every night, the trenches are destroyed before they reach the wire, and the garrison loses about a third fewer men in the most complete American victory of the war on the ground, which changes nothing in Washington; the brigade pulled from Thua Thien's hamlets to win it is missing when the Front returns to them (EV000-41). With no partial halt to trade, the decision of 31 March brings no talks, the May and August offensives are fought with no table in Paris, and the northern campaign above the 19th parallel costs about 40 aircraft over the gun belts (EV000-45, EV013-6) [X-013]. The halt of 1 November comes on history's date and opens the talks themselves (EV000-53), and Commando Hunt opens against a panhandle net built to be cut (EV000-55).

**How the phase ends:** At the end of 1968 the war has changed shape without changing direction. The VC in the South have lost much of their main and local forces and many of their cadres in the three offensives, and their recruitment has collapsed; the main-force war is now predominantly a PAVN war, and the parallel administration in the hamlets, though intact in much of the country, is under more pressure than at any time since 1959. The government in Saigon has survived Tet, mobilized, and begun with CORDS to push into the countryside; ARVN units fought better in February than anyone expected, though they remain dependent on American firepower and logistics. Against these gains, the United States has decided not to escalate further and to seek a negotiated way out; the bombing of the North has ended; and the American public's tolerance for casualties, measured in a year in which 14,592 Americans died by hostile action, has been spent [H40].

In Hanoi, the leadership has paid heavily for the General Offensive and turned back to protracted war for the moment, but has won what it most needed: an American president who will not reinforce and a successor committed to withdrawal. The Paris talks exist; the shape of the table is being settled. Phase IV opens with a new administration in Washington, a war in the countryside that the South is better placed to fight than it has been for years, and an American army whose withdrawal is now a matter of timing.

In this war the countryside is better placed than that, and the American decision of 1968 is unchanged, as is its timing.

- **The land.** About 900,000 hectares have been titled. The Front's Delta recruitment has fallen from a lower base, and its Delta battalions are filling with northerners earlier [X-001].
- **The infrastructure.** In the held belt it is weaker than anywhere since 1959. The Tet losses fell on a network already broken there, and the Front's district committees enter 1969 governing from further out than history's (EV012-8) [X-012].
- **The police.** The National Police numbers about 95,000, and every file it keeps is held under a destruction plan [X-002].
- **Phung Hoang.** It enters 1969 with five years of files, an audited count the press has learned to quote, and no quotas. The Front's Delta committees have lost a third of the leaders they sent into the towns (EV000-42, EV000-54) [X-006]. The Hue district files have shown what the national file would be worth to the enemy (EV000-44).
- **The combined command.** It found a traitor in its plans cell and has extended the two-layer plan to every corps (EV012-7). Hue was fought under one commander and ended five days early (EV000-44) [X-012].
- **The warning.** The files saw the towns' part of Tet and not its date (EV000-42) [X-CP03].

The RVNAF ends 1968 larger, with its battalions under commanders who held them through Tet and a board that has not stopped working [X-007]. It is armed throughout with weapons the historical army was still waiting for, a gap now closing from the historical side as the M16 reaches the ARVN in 1968 and the territorials in 1969 [X-004]. The mobilization's soldiers are trained to the regulars' standard and reached the field about a month late [X-009]. Its new platoons are led, in about fourteen cases in fifteen, by a man who passed the leader's course, against about two in three historically [X-010].

The mobilization's squads have no sergeants, its lieutenants were sergeants, and the academy's course is four weeks for the duration (EV000-51). The People's Self-Defense Force, which no course reached, has paid for the difference in Hau Nghia, Long An and Dinh Tuong (EV009-4). COSVN works among the officers the board passed over, and the Military Security Service keeps a second file on the board's officers, this time as targets (EV000-52).

About 2,150 rather than 2,788 ARVN soldiers died in the first wave. The hospitals of both armies are full of men who would have died on the historical course and are alive without a leg (F009-16) [X-009].

The PAVN leaves 1968 having learned that it does not lay siege to a position the Americans can measure. That is the one way of choosing its battles it has lost, and it chooses all the others [X-005]. The enemy's rear enters Phase IV counted. The surge after the halt is measured, and the first dry season of Commando Hunt is scored against the radar as well as the claims (EV003-5, EV000-55) [X-003]. The panhandle is harder to cut than history's, because the bombers taught its engineers how (EV000-55).

The northern campaign ends on 1 November, as history's did. It has lost about 810–880 aircraft rather than 922, and nothing is left in the North for it to destroy that the North could not rebuild in a night (EV000-53) [X-013]. The talks that open on 13 November are the talks history opened in May, six months late and on the same terms, and Nixon inherits them on history's date (EV000-48, EV000-53).

### Phase IV — Vietnamization and drawdown (Jan 1969 – Dec 1971)

Phase IV is the war of the American withdrawal. US strength peaks at about 539,000 in the first half of 1969 and falls to 474,000 at the end of that year, 336,000 at the end of 1970 and 158,000 at the end of 1971 [H40]. American deaths by hostile action fall with it, from about 9,414 in 1969 [D] to 4,221 in 1970 and 1,380 in 1971 [H40]. The Republic of Vietnam's armed forces grow to replace them: from about 897,000 in 1969 to 968,000 in 1970 and about 1,048,000 in 1971–72, the territorial Regional and Popular Forces growing fastest [H62]. The policy has a name, Vietnamization, and a premise: that the South, given equipment, time and American air power, can hold what the Americans leave.

The shape of the phase is a race between the withdrawal and the South's improvement, run while Hanoi rebuilds. In the countryside, the years 1969–71 are the best the government ever has. The VC, gutted by the 1968 offensives, return to protracted war on a reduced scale; pacification spreads under Phoenix and the territorial forces, into a countryside where the land programme of 1964 has already done most of its work (the Land to the Tiller law of 1970 does not happen, EV000-65); and by most indicators, including the ones the enemy cannot fake, the VC's hold on the population of the Delta and the coastal lowlands weakens. On the frontiers the war goes the other way. The North rebuilds its main forces, extends the Trail and its pipeline, and after Sihanouk's fall loses Sihanoukville but gains much of eastern Cambodia. The United States uses the time it has to strike the sanctuaries it had left alone, secretly from the air over Cambodia from March 1969, on the ground in Cambodia in May–June 1970, and through the ARVN alone in Laos in February–March 1971, and Congress closes the ground option behind each attempt.

At home the war's support is gone. The Moratorium, the Cambodian incursion and Kent State, and the publication of the Pentagon Papers mark a country that wants its army home, and an army in Vietnam, after 1969, that is itself coming apart under drugs, racial conflict and attacks on its own officers, waiting to leave a war it no longer expects to win [H]. In Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh dies in September 1969; the collective leadership around Le Duan negotiates secretly with Kissinger and, after the ARVN's defeat in Laos in 1971, decides to try once more for victory by conventional invasion.

In this war the phase follows the same course on the frontiers and in Washington [X-001]. In the countryside it starts further on. The land programme has nothing left to do by 1970 but the communal lands, and about 1,150,000 hectares are titled by the end of 1971 [X-001]. The Commission Against Corruption, which had outlived three governments behind the American lever, loses that lever as the Americans leave, and in July 1971 Thieu puts it under a presidential inspectorate after it opens an inquiry that reaches his own circle (EV001-8) [X-001].

The police and the provinces end the phase as the Commission does, working below the palace and reaching no higher (EV002-6); the historical gap narrows as the Republic builds after 1968 what this war had from 1964.

The enemy's rear is counted through the whole phase. The Cambodian incursion goes in on a map five years in the making and finds the caches in days rather than weeks, though Washington still names COSVN as the objective (EV000-66); Commando Hunt's claims are checked every night against a radar count, and the claim that the trucks destroyed exceeded the trucks that existed never survives a season (EV000-68); and Lam Son 719 goes in with an honest estimate of what waits for it, and fails for the reasons it failed historically (EV000-71).

The bombers' precision reaches the Cambodian base areas in 1969 and has a season of targets there before COSVN's rear services own nothing in the open (EV000-58). Over the Trail it adds a point or two to what Commando Hunt costs the enemy (EV000-68). In Lam Son 719 it teaches I Corps to build its defence around American bombs that will soon go home (EV000-71).

Three provisions of 1964 change the phase at three points. The American battalions go home as they came, whole, so the withdrawals do not scatter short-timers through the units that stay; the breakdown of discipline comes on its historical course regardless (EV000-60). The national Phung Hoang file, built since 1964 to the standard of a warrant, is taken into the palace's service with the Board and the Directorate in 1970–71 and consolidated in one building in Saigon for the election (EV002-6). And Phoenix comes before Congress in 1971 with an audited count since 1965 that its critics do not dispute (EV000-72).

The officer reforms reach the limit their memorandum named: the American lever. As the aid conditions are dropped with Vietnamization, the palace makes the board's general-officer list advisory in January 1970, keeps the board for everything below colonel, and in December 1970 answers a petition of colonels of the classes of 1957–59 by moving about forty of the army's best regimental and battalion commanders to staff and schools (EV007-5). Lam Son 719 goes into Laos weeks later with new commanders in two of the 1st Division's regiments and an Airborne brigade, and fails for the historical reasons, which were decided at corps and in Saigon (EV000-71). The battalions themselves are the best-led the Republic ever had.

Under the withdrawal, the Republic's own plants close the loop that Vietnamization would otherwise have left open: the American equipment handed over in 1969–71 goes into rebuild works and a signal depot that have run since 1966, and by the end of 1971 the RVNAF makes about two-fifths of its small-arms cartridges, most of its batteries and all of its wire, filled and powered from abroad (EV008-6). In the Delta the subsector advisers hand the call for fire to Vietnamese guns on Vietnamese sets before they leave (EV008-7). And the Directorate of Defence Industry goes to the palace with the Board, the list, the file and the Commission, keeping its output and losing its honesty (EV002-6).

The schooled sergeant meets the drawdown in both armies. In the American units that stay longest, the sergeant who enforces standards is the man the worst soldiers resent and some of them try to kill, and the schooled sergeant holds more squads together than history's without stopping the decay (EV010-5). In the Republic the gate on NCO promotion is the first of the army's merit rules that the palace breaks, by the National Day decree of 1 November 1970, in the same months it takes the board and the Directorate (EV010-6) [X-010]. The academy survives the advisers, because it was Vietnamese from the start.

In this war the home front of 1969–71 has no My Lai and a smaller draft. The Moratorium and the Mobilization of 1969 come on their dates without Hersh's story, and the Peers inquiry and the Calley trial do not happen (EV000-63, EV000-72) [X-011]. A quarter of the men the boards would have called have enlisted before their notices came, the boards send about 70,000 fewer notices in 1969 and about 40,000 fewer in 1970, and about one in four of the Army's draftees in the rifle companies of the drawdown chose to be there (EV010-5) [X-011]. None of it changes the withdrawal's schedule, which Washington set in 1969 for its own reasons; it changes the bitterness of the years in which the schedule ran (F011-10, F011-15).

**How the phase ends:** At the end of 1971 the United States has about 158,000 military personnel in Vietnam, its ground combat role is nearly over, and the last US combat divisions are leaving [H40]. The RVNAF numbers more than a million men under arms, well equipped and, in the territorial forces, more present in the hamlets than ever before [H62]. In the countryside the VC remain weaker than at any time since 1960 and weaker in the Delta than on the historical course; the land programme of 1964 has finished its work, with about 1,150,000 hectares titled, and the Land to the Tiller law of 1970 was never needed (EV000-65) [X-001]. The Commission survives below the rank of minister and general and no longer above it (EV001-8) [X-001]. The gains are real, and the government measures them.

On the frontiers the balance is the reverse. The PAVN has rebuilt its main forces, extended the Trail, lost Sihanoukville and replaced it, and watched the ARVN's best divisions fail in Laos. The secret channel in Paris is deadlocked on Thieu's removal and on the PAVN's presence in the South. In Hanoi, after Lam Son 719, the Politburo has decided to stake the next year on a conventional invasion across the DMZ, from Laos into the Central Highlands and from Cambodia towards Saigon, timed to an American election year and to the near completion of the American withdrawal [H56] [H]. Phase V asks whether the South can stop it with American air power and no American ground troops.

The posts, the census and the district Special Branch sections stand under a palace that chooses the loyal among the competent; what the Republic keeps from 1964 is the chiefs' experience and four extra years of files (EV002-6) [X-002].

The radar's ledger has made the interdiction debate honest and changed nothing it was about: the Trail is larger than ever, and the aircraft that count it will leave with the Americans (EV000-68) [X-003].

The ARVN's I Corps ends the phase believing, on the evidence of Lolo and Sophia, that a besieged base under American bombers holds (EV000-71). It is true, and it is the belief that will cost it most when the bombers go [X-005].

Phung Hoang ends 1971 with an audited count of about 63,000 neutralized since 1965 and a national file of about 230,000 names in one building in Saigon, serving the President as well as the war (EV000-72, EV002-6) [X-006]. About 3,500 selected advisers remain, with the territorials and the province teams more than with the divisions; the American battalions have gone home whole and their discipline has decayed on its historical course (EV000-60) [X-006].

The board ends 1971 as the machinery of the army below colonel and nothing above it (EV007-5) [X-007]. The battalions that went into Laos came out better than the operation did (EV000-71).

The RVNAF enters 1972 with a closed rebuild loop and a domestic share that covers about two-fifths of its small-arms cartridges, a third of its 105mm rounds and most of its batteries, under a Directorate the palace now runs (EV008-6, EV002-6) [X-008]. The districts of the Delta call Vietnamese guns on Vietnamese sets (EV008-7). The base has not yet been tested by a year without American supply.

The NCO academy at Nha Trang ends 1971 Vietnamese, as it began, with its American advisers gone and its course whole; the gate on promotion, broken by decree, has been half restored by the training command (EV010-6) [X-010]. The American NCO corps leaves schooled and spent (EV010-5).

The 81st Gunship Wing ends 1971 holding the night over about two-thirds of the posts the Ghostriders held, through cloud on the coast where they never could, and in Vietnamese; the posts beyond its reach are attacked more often as the Americans leave (EV015-6, EV008-7) [X-015].

### Phase V — The Easter Offensive and Linebacker (Jan 1972 – Dec 1972)

*End of phase against the historical state: POP.night_control +1 to +4 against history (low) · POP.night_control.I_corps -1 to +1 against history (low) · POP.night_control.II_corps -1 to +1 against history (low) · POP.night_control.III_corps +2 to +5 against history (low) · POP.night_control.IV_corps +3 to +6 against history (low) · TRAIL.tonnage_arriving -10% to 0% against history (low) · ARVN.self_sufficiency.fire_support -8 to 0 against history (low).*

1972 is the test of Vietnamization, and the answer it gives is exact: the Republic of Vietnam can stop a full PAVN conventional offensive with American air power and American advisers, and cannot do it without them. On 30 March the PAVN opens the largest offensive of the war, called the Nguyen Hue Offensive in Hanoi and the Easter Offensive in the West, with about fourteen divisions and hundreds of tanks [H] on three main fronts: across the DMZ into Quang Tri, from Laos and Cambodia into the Central Highlands at Kontum, and from Cambodia down Route 13 at An Loc towards Saigon [H64]. US ground strength has fallen to about 69,000 men, few of them combat troops, and is on its way to 27,000 [H64]. US air power returns in strength: B-52s and tactical aircraft over the battlefields of the South, and, for the first time since 1968, a bombing campaign against the North without most of Rolling Thunder's restrictions, with the mining of Haiphong.

The shape of the phase is a near-collapse in the spring and a recovery in the summer. Quang Tri Province falls on 1–2 May; Kontum and An Loc are besieged and held by narrow margins and B-52s; and by the autumn the ARVN, under better commanders, has retaken Quang Tri City. The PAVN loses most of the armour it committed and, by most estimates, about 100,000 men, killed and wounded, while keeping about a tenth of the South's territory, mostly thinly populated border regions in the west [H64]. The offensive creates almost a million refugees and kills more than 25,000 civilians [H64]. Its political result is the one Hanoi needed: a settlement on terms that leave PAVN troops in the South. The year ends with the October draft agreement, Thieu's refusal of it, and the eleven days of Linebacker II.

In this war the armour of the Easter Offensive is seen before it crosses the DMZ and is struck by radar-bombing B-52s through the cloud that grounded the fighter-bombers (EV000-74); Linebacker chooses from target folders seven years in the making and counts the effect of the mining on the North's own roads (EV000-75); and at An Loc the B-52 boxes of 10–12 May fall on assembly areas the radar shows (EV000-76). Quang Tri still falls, An Loc and Kontum still hold, and the lessons both sides draw are the historical ones.

The B-52J's year is this one. Freedom Train drops the Thanh Hoa bridge on its first night (EV000-75); the siege box breaks the penetration of An Loc on 12 May and the assault on Kontum short of the wire, and Kontum is secure five days early (EV000-76, EV000-77); and Linebacker II loses about six bombers rather than fifteen and does not strike Bach Mai or Kham Thien Street (EV000-82). Quang Tri still falls, and the terms of January are the terms of October.

The officer reforms meet the offensive at regiment and battalion, and the offensive is decided above them. On the DMZ front the 3rd Division's battalions, under commanders the board chose, give ground in better order than history's, and the 56th Regiment's commander, a board-chosen officer with a hero's record from Hue, surrenders Camp Carroll all the same (EV000-74). At Quang Tri the contradictory orders of the corps and the division are the historical orders, and the division still breaks, but one of its regiments holds the road south open long enough to bring out its column (EV000-78). At Tan Canh more of the 22nd Division gets out, and Kontum and An Loc are held as before (EV000-77). The army fights the year as it was taught to fight, with American air at the centre of every plan, and depends on it more for having learned to use it well (F007-23).

**How the phase ends:** At the end of 1972 the war is on the verge of a settlement that both governments in Vietnam regard as provisional. The Easter Offensive has failed to destroy the ARVN or the Thieu government, at a cost to the PAVN of most of the armour it committed (by one count 134 T-54s, 56 PT-76s and 60 T-34s) and, on the historical count, about 100,000 men [H64]. The ARVN has held at An Loc and Kontum and retaken Quang Tri City, but has lost Quang Tri north of the Thach Han, the western Highlands and the border areas of III Corps, and its losses are given variously from about 10,000 killed to about 39,000 dead in the period [H64]. Almost a million South Vietnamese have been made refugees, about 600,000 of them in government camps [H64].

In this war the PAVN's losses for the year are higher than that count, and higher in particular formations. The GBU-38 cells added perhaps a fifth to the losses of the B-2 Front's divisions around An Loc, the siege box destroyed about a third of the guns brought to Kontum before the assault and broke the 320th Division's assault short of the wire, and the radar-bombing of the armour on the DMZ destroyed some 20–30 vehicles before they reached the firebases (EV000-74, EV000-76, EV000-77) [X-005]. Taken together I put the PAVN's killed and wounded in 1972 at about 7,000–10,000 above the historical figure, roughly a tenth more, concentrated in the 5th, 7th and 9th Divisions and the 320th and 2nd Divisions, which are the formations that will fight Phuoc Long, Ban Me Thuot and Xuan Loc [X-MT01]. The North replaces that difference within its flow of men for 1973 [E: one to two months of a replacement flow to the South of the order of 100,000 men a year or more in 1973–74]. What it does not replace as quickly is the experienced cadre killed in the measured assaults, and the 7th and 9th Divisions enter 1974 with greener companies than history's [X-MT01].

The countryside ends 1972 in two parts. Where a PAVN division came into the peopled lowlands, in northern Binh Dinh and Quang Tri, the gains of 1964–71 were lost and the hamlets returned to the state history left them in (EVMT01-1). In the held belt of the Delta and around Saigon the posts held through the year, the Front's infrastructure inside the post line did not return, and the files that will open the "war of the flags" survived intact (EVMT01-2). In Saigon the decree powers and the end of the hamlet elections took back the government's claim to the hamlets' consent, as they did historically (EVMT01-3). The historical land programme has by now distributed about a million hectares of its own, and the margin of the 1964 titling over history has narrowed to its six years of head start and the councils that confirmed it [H] [X-MT01]. Night control and the Front's weakness in the held belt remain one band better than history's; the government's legitimacy has returned to history's; and the Special Branch's knowledge of the infrastructure, which the historical police and Phoenix had largely caught up with by 1972, is one band better rather than two [X-MT01].

The lesson both sides draw is the same. The ARVN held where American air power was decisive, at An Loc and Kontum, and where American advisers coordinated it; it broke where its leadership failed, at Quang Tri and Tan Canh. The settlement about to be signed removes the American advisers and the American air power and leaves the PAVN in the South, while the North's air defences and economy recover. Hanoi needs only to rebuild, wait for the Americans to be gone, and choose its time.

The aircraft are still flying at the end of 1972, still American, and under the agreement about to be signed they will soon have no American strike force to cue. The Republic keeps nothing of them: no aircraft, no exploitation cells, no practice in using either.

The ARVN has held An Loc and Kontum more cheaply than history's, and has learned more completely that it holds besieged towns with American bombers measured onto the enemy by American analysts (EV000-76, EV000-77). The agreement about to be signed takes both away. The Republic enters 1973 more confident than history's and more dependent [X-005].

The ARVN's regiments and battalions have fought the offensive better than history's, and its divisions and corps no better: Quang Tri was lost by orders, and the column on Highway 1 was saved in part by a regiment (EV000-78). It has learned, from An Loc and Kontum, to use American air with an educated staff's precision, and it has no air of its own that its plans can rest on (F007-23) [X-007].

### Phase VI — Paris, the endgame, and 1975 (Jan 1973 – Dec 1975)

*End of phase against the historical state: POP.night_control 35–55 (history 0; low) · POP.night_control.II_corps 10–25 (history 0; low) · POP.night_control.III_corps 60–80 (history 0; low) · POP.night_control.IV_corps 68–87 (history 0; low) · POP.displacement +300 to +600 against history (low) · POP.gvn_legitimacy 0 to +5 against history (low) · GVN.political_stability 0 (history 2; low) · VCI.strength -40% to -15% against history (low) · ENEMY.engagement_control -5 to +2 against history (low) · TRAIL.tonnage_arriving -20% to +20% against history (low) · ARVN.effectiveness -35% to -15% against history (low) · ARVN.self_sufficiency +6 to +12 against history (low) · ARVN.self_sufficiency.logistics +3 to +8 against history (low) · ARVN.self_sufficiency.fire_support +5 to +12 against history (low) · US.casualties 0 (history 2; high) · US.political_tolerance 3 (history 2; low) · US.political_tolerance.public 0 to +2 against history (medium) · US.political_tolerance.congress 950–1,275 (history 700; medium) · US.political_tolerance.administration 4 (history 3; medium) · NEGOT.position 3 (history 1; low).*

Phase VI is the war without the Americans. The Paris Agreement of January 1973 takes US forces out and returns the prisoners; it leaves the PAVN in the South, the Thieu government in Saigon, and the war to be decided between them. The ceasefire never holds. In 1973 Saigon is on the offensive, recovering hamlets and roads, while the North rebuilds; in 1974 the two are evenly matched, and the ARVN, short of ammunition, fuel and spare parts as American aid falls, bleeds in a war of attrition it cannot sustain; in January 1975 the North tests whether the United States will respond to the seizure of a province, and when it does not, it commits its army to the Highlands [H72].

The shape of the phase is three slow years and a fast spring. The constraints that bind the American role are now law, not policy: the Case–Church amendment ends all US combat activity in Indochina from 15 August 1973, and Congress cuts military aid. In Hanoi, the 21st Plenum of October 1973 returns to revolutionary violence, and the PAVN builds a road network east of the mountains, a fuel pipeline into the South and an army of corps. In Saigon, the economy, hit by the oil shock and the departure of the Americans whose spending had sustained it, and a government that has narrowed its base, face the offensive of 1975 with an army spread thin across the whole country.

In this war the army that fights the last three years has been built for ten years around the belt-fed gun and the abundance of American ammunition, and the ration of 1974 finds it more dependent on volume than the historical one (EV000-89). It fights the attrition of 1974 with better weapons than its enemy and too few rounds to use them, and the hoards it builds against the ration are lost with Hue and the Highlands (EV000-91, EV000-94, EV000-95).

The bombers leave in August 1973 without bombing Neak Luong, and the coordinate cell is disbanded with nothing in the VNAF to send coordinates to (EV000-86). The ARVN fights 1974 and the defence of Phuoc Long with plans written for an air force that no longer comes, and loses Thuong Duc and Phuoc Long as history did, with its officers knowing exactly what they lack (EV000-91, EV000-92).

Phung Hoang outlives the Americans as a Vietnamese programme and helps the Republic's offensive of 1973 in the Delta; its national file, consolidated in Saigon since 1971, is still in the Central Intelligence Organization's building at the end of 1975, and the province files of Quang Ngai and Quang Tin are taken when those provinces fall in March (EV000-84, EV000-94, EV000-98). The advisers are gone in March 1973, and nothing of their eighteen months survives them but the counterparts who remember them.

The officer reforms leave the Republic in its last three years an officer corps that knows precisely what it lacks. Its battalion and regimental commanders, educated on a doctrine built around American fire, plan the battles of 1974 for a weight of fire the ration no longer allows (EV000-91). Its staff college writes, in November 1974, the only serious plan the Republic ever had for a defence on reduced resources; in March 1975 the President rejects it entirely and orders everything held, and its method is used a year late, for the evacuation of Da Nang in May (EV000-95, EV011-3).

In this war the last ration also fell on an army that made two-fifths of its own small-arms ammunition, a third of its 105mm rounds and nearly all of its radio batteries, from imported powder and semiconductors (EV000-89). The domestic plants stretched each ammunition and communications dollar, made the attrition of 1974 somewhat cheaper and changed no position the PAVN chose to take (EV000-91), gave Phuoc Long more rounds than it could fire (EV000-92), and in 1975 were still the Republic's (EV011-3).

In this war there is no Watergate, and the President who wrote Thieu his promises is in office to the end of the record. Case–Church passes as historically, so that the bombers he promised cannot lawfully return, but the War Powers Resolution fails in the House, the Republicans of 1974 do not desert him, the midterm costs his party about 22 House seats instead of 49, and the fiscal 1975 appropriation is about $950 million, which the Republic's own plants stretch to buy about what $1.2 billion bought historically (EV000-86, EV000-89, EV011-1) [X-011]. The Republic fights 1974 near the 1973 allowance. In March 1975, with a year's fuel and a President who has asked Congress for its bombers and been refused, Thieu refuses the Dalat staff college's withdrawal and orders the Highlands and I Corps held (F011-20); the Highlands are lost in five weeks instead of ten days and Hue in an ordered withdrawal in April, and on 31 March the Politburo, which historically resolved on 25 March to take Saigon before the rains, has no double collapse to resolve on and puts Saigon back to the dry season of 1975–76 (EV000-94, EV000-95, EVMT01-4) [X-011]. The Republic ends 1975 smaller, holding III and IV Corps and the coast from Nha Trang south, with its general reserve brought back from Da Nang by sea and its fall expected in the first months of 1976 (EV011-3) [X-011].

- EVMT01-4 · The Politburo's calendar: Saigon after the rains · 25 Mar – 14 Apr 1975 · Hanoi and the roads south · HIST-ALT
- EV000-96 · Xuan Loc · 9–21 Apr 1975 · Xuan Loc, Long Khanh Province, northeast of Saigon · CANCELLED
- EV000-97 · The President's request; Thieu stays · 10–30 Apr 1975 · Saigon and Washington · HIST-ALT
- EV000-98 · The fall of Saigon · 29–30 Apr 1975 · Saigon · CANCELLED
- EV011-3 · Operation SOUTHERN WALL and the rains · 1 May – 31 Dec 1975 · Da Nang, Qui Nhon and the central coast; Saigon; Hanoi and the strategic road · NEW

**How the phase ends:** In this war Phase VI does not end with the fall of Saigon. On 31 December 1975 the Republic of Vietnam holds III and IV Corps, the coast from Nha Trang south and about half the population of 1974; the PAVN holds the Highlands, I Corps and the central coast north of Khanh Hoa, and five corps are assembled for an offensive on the capital in the first months of 1976 (EV011-3) [X-011]. That is a conclusion and not an assumption. The date of 30 April 1975 was set in Hanoi by a resolution to finish before the rains, and the resolution was made possible by the double collapse of I and II Corps in the second half of March; in this war Thieu's decision of 11–14 March went the other way, the Highlands were lost in a five-week siege instead of a ten-day rout, Hue in an ordered withdrawal on 18 April instead of a collapse on 25 March, and the Politburo, without a collapse to resolve on, put Saigon back to the dry season (EV000-94, EV000-95, EVMT01-4) [X-011]. The mechanism was political and at the top: a President in Washington who did not fall, an appropriation near the 1974 level, and a President in Saigon who believed, on that evidence, that he need not give anything up (F011-20, F011-21). It bought a season, and it was bought at a price. The refusal of the Dalat study cost the Republic half its Highland force and the 2nd Division, which a planned withdrawal in the dry season would have saved, and its reserve spent the spring at Da Nang, five hundred kilometres from the capital, until SOUTHERN WALL brought it home in May.

The Republic that enters 1976 is not the historical Republic, and it is not a Republic that has survived. Its fall is expected in the dry season of 1976, by my estimate between February and May, from an offensive on the capital by five corps that it has a rebuilt reserve, a full arsenal, its Delta and its capital's belt to meet, and no American air power (EV011-3) [X-011]. Rung (b) by the test of rules/RUNGS.toml, because Saigon stands past 30 April 1975; the outcome in its own terms is a reprieve of about a year, and the record ends before it is spent. The Paris Agreement had removed the American forces and kept the PAVN in the South; Congress had written the end of American combat into law and would not unwrite it for a President who asked; American military aid had fallen less than history's but had fallen; and the government in Saigon, more stable than at any time since 1963, faced an enemy that had rebuilt after 1972 and chose its moment, and then chose to wait.

At the end of 1974, on the eve of Phuoc Long, the held belt of the Delta and the Saigon region was held at night more firmly than history's, and the Front's district committees there had lost about twice the historical share of their members in 1973 (EV000-84) [X-006]; the Special Branch's knowledge of the infrastructure was still the better for its ten years of files; the government's standing in the hamlets was history's, after the decrees of 1972; the army's battalions were better led and its divisions and corps no better; and the army as a whole was more dependent than history's on American fire it no longer had, and knew it (EV000-91, EV000-92) [X-MT01]. In this war the army had also fought 1974 near the 1973 allowance, with its aircraft flying and its relief columns fuelled, and lost perhaps 2,500–6,500 fewer men in the year than history's 30,000, a judgment on the two rates named in EV000-91 [X-008] [X-011]. At the end of 1975 the held belt and the files are still the Republic's, and the end vector measures a state that still exists.

Hanoi's posture never changed. It was committed to armed reunification throughout, from the Ninth Plenum of December 1963 to the resolution of October 1975 that set the offensive on Saigon for 1976, through the losses of 1965–68 and 1972 and the delay of 1975, and it accepted the Paris Agreement as a step towards that end. The timing of its campaign was its own, set by its army's road, the season and, in March 1975, by a map that did not offer it the collapse history had (EVMT01-4). The US war in Vietnam, from the advisory years to 1973, cost more than 58,000 American dead [H]. The Vietnamese dead, military and civilian, northern and southern, are counted in the millions by most estimates, and the record of them is less precise than the record of the Americans [H].

The squad guns and the marksmen's rifles of the ARVN's II Corps and of the 1st and 2nd Divisions are in the PAVN's hands by the end of the spring, with the hoards of Quang Ngai and the Highlands; the hoard at Hue was destroyed in place, and the hoards of III and IV Corps are still the Republic's [X-004] [X-011].

The Republic's defence of every besieged town had been built since 1971 around American bombers and American coordinates, and both were gone by the end of 1973 (EV000-86, EV000-92) [X-005]. At Pleiku in April 1975 it fought a siege without them, on fuel and rounds, and held three weeks (EV000-95).

The officers the reforms made fought 1975 as well as any part of the RVNAF fought it. Their best staff plan was refused in March and used in May, for SOUTHERN WALL and the rebuilding of the reserve (EV000-95, EV011-3). The board's files, with the evaluation report of every officer since 1964, are in the Joint General Staff's compound at the end of 1975 [X-007] [X-011].

The Republic's own plants stretched its aid dollar by about a third to two-fifths, kept its radios on the air through 1974, and in 1975 were the arsenal of an army that had lost its northern hoards; they shortened no collapse and lengthened none, because the spring of 1975 was decided by orders, families and an enemy who chose his ground, and at the end of the year they are still the Republic's (EV000-89, EVMT01-4, EV011-3) [X-008] [X-011].

The Republic's gunships fought the territorial war of 1973–74 at night and won most of it where they reached, in the Delta's canal posts and the coast's lowlands (EV000-84, EV015-8); they could not fly over the PAVN's divisions in 1974 or 1975, because the divisions brought their own air defence (EV000-91, EV000-95) [X-015].

# Card 016 — Glock 21 pistol with tritium night sights and SureFire X300 Turbo light: every US and RVNAF handgun replaced from 1964, and the standard handgun of the National Police

*Memorandum 016 · status part2 · full record: memos/016/ · generated by fie.py*

## P016a · Glock 21 Gen5 MOS .45 Auto pistol in its 2026 configuration (13-round magazine, Glock factory tritium night sights (GNS), accessory rail) with a SureFire X300T Turbo weapon light (650 lumens, 66,000 candela, two 123A lithium cells) mounted on every pistol, carried in a light-bearing duty holster; replacing every M1911A1, M1917, .38 revolver and other handgun of the US forces in Southeast Asia and of the RVNAF (ARVN, VNAF, VNN, VNMC, Regional and Popular Forces), and issued as the standard handgun of the National Police and the National Police Field Force; the police keep their historical long arms (E05)
about 55,000–60,000 pistols and lights in theater in 1964, rising to about 230,000–250,000 at the 1969–72 peak, plus a 10% float [E: D1; about one pistol per eight US personnel in theater, one per ten RVNAF regulars, one per twenty-five territorials and one per National Policeman, against the strengths in S6, S7 and the record] · spaces ~40–60 [E: D2; a US armament and training detachment for the RVNAF and police issue in 1964, absorbed into the existing advisory structure after 1966; no ceiling (CONFIG troop_ceiling = NONE)] · arrives 1964-01-01 · SECURE, FIX, SUBVERT · ground

**Key figures.**
- Glock 21 Gen5 MOS, .45 Auto, 13-round magazine, 205 mm long, 117 mm barrel, 1,095 g loaded; trigger 26 N; no manual safety [M016·S1]
- Glock factory tritium night sights (GNS), 174 mm sight radius; brightness about halved by 1976 [M016·S1] [E: 12.3-year half-life]
- SureFire X300T Turbo: 650 lumens, 66,000 candela, 514 m beam, 1.5 h on two 123A lithium cells, 124.7 g, IPX7 [M016·S2]
- Holders: about 55,000–57,000 in 1964 and about 230,000–235,000 at the 1969–72 peak, plus a 10% float; about three-quarters Vietnamese in 1964 [E: D1]
- Replaces the M1911A1 (7 rounds, Second World War production), the police's .38 revolvers (6 rounds) and every other US and RVNAF handgun; same .45 ball round as the M1911A1 and M3A1 [M016·S8] [E: D3]
- Police long arms unchanged (E05); the PRUs, CIDG, militia and PSDF not covered [M002·S1] [U]
- About 1.5–2.0 million 123A cells a year at the peak, all American supply [E: D8]
- About 40–60 US spaces in 1964–65 for training and issue; none after 1966 [E: D2]
- First-shot hit chance at 7–15 m in darkness about twice history's, low confidence [E: D13]

**Negative specification.** - It does not defend a post, a hamlet or a perimeter. A pistol is the weapon of the last few metres, and nothing about it changes who holds a hamlet after dark.
- It does not find anyone. It touches neither the main force nor the identification of the VCI (A6); it helps only at the moment of arrest or clearance, after someone else has done the finding.
- It does not rearm the police. Under erratum E05 the constable keeps his carbine and the Police Field Force its carbines, BARs and M79s; only the handgun changes.
- It does not reach the CIDG, the PRUs, the hamlet militia, the People's Self-Defense Force or third-country forces.
- It carries no suppressor. The suppressed revolvers, the High Standard HD .22s and the Smith & Wesson Mk 22 Mod 0 pistols of the tunnel clearers and raiders are withdrawn with the rest, and the standard Glock 21 is louder underground than they were.
- It does not fit small hands well. Its grip is one of the largest of any service pistol, and many Vietnamese and some American holders shoot it less well than they shot the slimmer M1911A1.
- Its light betrays its user at night when misused; it is a weapon light, not a flashlight.
- Its light needs American 123A lithium cells. The Republic cannot make them, and the light dies with the cell supply.
- It has no manual safety; in poorly trained hands it produces negligent discharges.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the dark doorway and the dark tunnel: the man who waited in a hut or a tunnel bend for the searcher with a flashlight in one hand now faces a light on the gun, glowing sights and thirteen rounds. It also denies the assassin his easiest assumption, that the village official or the constable has six rounds and no light. It gives the enemy something back: every pistol lost with a killed official or an overrun post is a prized weapon for the Front's cadres and security sections.

**Verdict.** This is a modest provision that does real good at the very bottom of the war, and I will not dress it up. The Glock 21 with night sights and a light is a better pistol than the M1911A1 in every way except the size of its grip, and for the constable it is a much better weapon than the .38 he replaces. Its effect is concentrated where pistols are actually used: in tunnels, in night arrests and house searches, in the last minutes of an overrun bunker, and in the hands of a downed pilot. A tunnel clearer at Cu Chi now goes into the dark with the light on his muzzle and his other hand free. A district police sergeant at a door at 0300 can see whether the man inside is holding a grenade or a child. Those men will live, and arrest instead of kill, a little more often. It will not change who holds the hamlets, who initiates the war's fights, or the end state, and I expect its effect on the American dead to be measured in dozens a year, not hundreds. Its costs are small and real: a cell supply the Republic cannot make, negligent discharges in the first year, a grip too large for many Vietnamese hands, and better pistols for the Front's assassins wherever an official dies with one on his belt.

**Pushes:** US.casualties -15 to -10 [US killed by hostile action in the calendar year in which the phase ends (Phase I: 1965)] by the end of P2 (low), FIND.vci +0.1 to +0.15 [VCI neutralised a year who were on a prior target list, district level or above, thousands] by the end of P3 (low), POP.civilian_harm -0.2 to -0.15 [civilian dead and wounded in the South from all sides' operations, thousands a year] by the end of P2 (low) · **Depends on:** GVN.police, ARVN.effectiveness.night_ops, POP.night_control, RFPF.effectiveness.outpost_defence, VCI.strength, LOG.distribution, ARVN.self_sufficiency.maintenance, SUBVERT.defection, INTEL.penetration

- P016a × P015a, P015b: the post commander's light is the wrong signal to a gunship overhead; the post marks its wall with its own strobes and fires, not with weapon lights, which the crews cannot tell from the enemy's (F016-7)


## Standing directives

- **DIRCP01-1** · In each Part 3, take at least one causal chain from an earlier memorandum whose later links fall in a phase this memorandum revises, and test it against the war as now written; where the new provision or free play makes it resolve differently, say so in the chain review and let it (every chain in memoranda 001–005 resolved as predicted, which is more likely tidiness than foresight)
- **DIRCP01-2** · A war-wide figure for lives saved, or any war-wide count built from a rate, must be shown at work in at least two dated events in the chapters before a later memorandum repeats it; until then it is cited as a judgment resting on its rate, with the rate named (CP01 calibration of the [X-004] lives-saved figure)
- **DIRMT01-1** · In every §4.N, state the date of the Republic's fall as its own estimate, separately from the rung: a window, the mechanisms in the cumulative force that pull it earlier and those that pull it later, and which dominate and why; "on the historical timeline" may be written only as the conclusion of that test, and a change of date is reported as a change of date and does not by itself move the rung between (a) and (b) while the ladder's overlap stands (the historical fall, twenty-five months after the last American combat troops left, satisfies the words of rung (b), and seven memoranda have kept (a) and (b) apart by the date alone)
- **DIRMT01-2** · In every §4.N, carry a running sum of the sub-band estimates that all memoranda so far have made on the same variable (American dead, ARVN battalions not lost, and the like), tagged as exercise judgments with their rates named, and say whether the sum crosses a band; and treat the American aid appropriation of 1974 and the refusal of April 1975 as events a provision can change, not as history to be carried (each memorandum judged its own saving of American lives alone, and the 1974 vote was never examined)
- **DIRMT01-3** · Where a chapter's end vector returns a variable to the historical state from a non-zero band in the phase before, the chapter must contain the dated events that produce the convergence; and in every memorandum that revises Phase VI, state in the phase's analysis the Republic's state at the end of 1974, before the last offensive, because the phase's end vector is measured after the fall and cannot record anything the fall erased (Phase V returned four countryside variables to history with no sentence on the countryside, and Phase VI's vector is blind by construction)
- **DIRMT01-4** · Where a memorandum alters an event and keeps its historical outcome, name what absorbs the difference (the enemy's choice to bypass or decline, a decision above the level the provision reached, an external fixed by law or by another government) and show it in the event; "as historically" is a conclusion, never a mechanism (in Phase VI at least six altered events in the last campaign restore the historical outcome by statement)
- **DIRMT01-5** · Where a perverse effect or a capture undoes a gain, state the net in both directions with its weight, and where several provisions' institutions fall to the same mechanism in the same years, judge them together before judging each alone (four institutions from four memoranda fall to the lapse of the American lever in 1970–71, each judged alone, and every memorandum closes on the gain undone)

- **DIRMT01-8** · Every memorandum touching the countryside states its effect separately for the Delta, the coastal lowlands of I and II Corps, the Highlands and their peoples, and the Saigon belt, and names a place in each where the effect is shown or says why there is none (the Delta was written as a footnote, the Montagnards appear twice and FULRO never, and Binh Dinh vanished from the record after 1967)
- **DIRMT01-9** · Every provision touching the reliability of the ARVN or the territorial forces addresses the soldier's family: where it lives, what his pay buys after inflation, and what happens to it when the unit moves or the front gives way (the corps of 1975 dissolved toward their families, and no memorandum had treated them)
